title: White rice: calories, carbs and nutrition

seo.title: White rice: calories, carbs and nutrition
seo.meta_description: Cooked white rice provides about 130 calories and 28 g carbohydrate per 100 g, with little fat or fiber. Dry rice looks much more calorie-dense because it contains far less water.
seo.search_intent: Explain the nutrition of cooked white rice and why dry and cooked values differ so much.

excerpt: Cooked white rice provides about 130 calories and 28 g carbohydrate per 100 g, with very little fat and fiber. Dry rice looks far more calorie-dense per 100 g because cooking adds water and spreads the same energy across a heavier portion.
content_html:
Cooked white rice can look surprisingly light on a nutrition chart because much of its cooked weight is water. That is why two numbers need to stay separate: 100 g dry rice and 100 g cooked rice are not nutritionally concentrated to the same degree.

What cooked white rice provides

A USDA reference for cooked long-grain white rice provides about 130 calories, 28.2 g carbohydrate, 2.7 g protein and 0.4 g fiber per 100 g. Fat is very low, around 0.3 g.

Per 100 g cookedApproximate amount
Calories130 kcal
Carbohydrate28.2 g
Protein2.7 g
Fat0.3 g
Fiber0.4 g

Most of the energy comes from starch. White rice is not especially high in protein or fat, and refining removes much of the fiber-containing bran.

Why dry rice looks so much higher in calories

Dry long-grain white rice is around 365 calories and 80 g carbohydrate per 100 g in a USDA reference. Cooking adds water and weight without creating calories. The same dry rice therefore spreads its energy across a much heavier cooked portion.

A 70 g dry portion may finish at roughly two to three times that weight depending on the rice and cooking method. The calories have not vanished; the concentration has changed.

What does a normal serving look like?

A 150 g cooked portion of the reference rice provides about 195 calories and 42 g carbohydrate. At 200 g, that becomes roughly 260 calories and 56 g carbohydrate.

That is why “a bowl of rice” can mean very different nutrition numbers depending on the actual amount.

What refining changes

Milling removes the bran and germ, lowering fiber and removing some naturally occurring vitamins and minerals. In the United States, enriched white rice often has iron and several B vitamins added back, so micronutrient values differ between enriched and unenriched products.

Is white rice nutritionally empty?

No. It supplies carbohydrate and energy and can be part of a balanced meal. It simply does not provide much fiber and is less micronutrient-dense than an intact whole grain in several respects.

Pairing rice with beans, vegetables, eggs, fish, meat or tofu changes the meal substantially by adding protein, fiber, fat and micronutrients.

Cooling cooked rice and reheating it later can increase the amount of resistant starch slightly, but the effect should not be exaggerated. It does not turn white rice into a high-fiber food, and the total carbohydrate remains substantial. The bigger practical differences usually come from portion size and what the rice is served with.

Food safety is important because cooked rice can support Bacillus cereus if it sits warm for too long. Leftover rice should be cooled promptly, refrigerated, and reheated thoroughly rather than being left on the counter for hours. The problem is not that rice is uniquely dangerous, but that its spores can survive cooking and grow if storage is poor.

Pairing rice with protein, vegetables, and legumes changes the meal far more than focusing on the grain alone. Beans with rice add fiber and protein; vegetables add volume and micronutrients; eggs, fish, tofu, or poultry can make the plate more balanced. This also slows eating and may reduce the need for a very large rice portion.

White rice can be especially useful when a low-fiber, easily digested carbohydrate is desired, during some gastrointestinal problems or before certain types of exercise. Whole grains have advantages in fiber and micronutrients, but choosing white rice sometimes is not a nutritional failure when the overall diet is varied.

Rice type changes texture and glycemic response. Long-grain, basmati, jasmine, and short-grain varieties differ in starch composition, especially the balance of amylose and amylopectin. That affects stickiness and can influence how quickly the carbohydrate is digested, although preparation and meal composition still matter.

Rinsing rice mainly removes surface starch and can change texture; it does not wash away most of the carbohydrate. Enriched rice is a special case because aggressive rinsing may remove some added surface nutrients in products where fortification is applied externally. Package directions are useful when enrichment matters.

The number worth remembering

For plain cooked white rice, about 130 calories and 28 g carbohydrate per 100 g is a useful reference. Portion size and how much water the rice absorbed are the main reasons your bowl may differ.

faq.question: How many calories are in 100 g cooked white rice?
faq.answer: A USDA reference lists about 130 calories per 100 g cooked.

faq.question: How many carbs are in cooked white rice?
faq.answer: About 28 g carbohydrate per 100 g in the reference used here.

faq.question: Why does dry rice have more calories per 100 g?
faq.answer: Dry rice contains far less water. Cooking adds water and spreads the same energy over a heavier final weight.
